title: Merge Sorted Array
directAnswer: Merge nums2 into nums1 in place. The naive answer copies both into a buffer and sorts (O((m+n)log(m+n))); the canonical answer merges from the BACK with three pointers (i=m−1, j=n−1, k=m+n−1), writing the larger element into the tail so you never overwrite an unread value in nums1.

rules: Fill from the **back** (`k = m+n-1`), not the front — the free space in `nums1` lives at the tail.
The loop ends when `j` (the `nums2` pointer) is exhausted — leftover `nums1` elements are **already in place**.
Guard `i >= 0` inside the comparison so you don't read `nums1[-1]` when `nums1` runs out first.
Use the real lengths `m` and `n`, not `nums1.length` — `nums1` is padded with zeros you must ignore.
Pick the **larger** of the two candidates for the tail slot, since we're filling largest-first.
No extra array needed — this is `O(1)` space, which is the whole point of merging backwards.
whenToUse: Two **sorted** sequences that must become one sorted sequence
One container has trailing free space to absorb the other in place
You want `O(m+n)` time without an auxiliary buffer
The merge step of merge sort, or k-way merge generalisations
antiSignals: Inputs are unsorted → sort first, or this trick buys nothing
No spare room in the destination → you genuinely need an output array
You need to merge thousands of lists → use a heap (k-way merge)
Order doesn't matter → just concatenate and sort
remember.takeaway: When you must merge into a buffer that already holds one of the inputs, fill from the back. Writing largest-first into the tail guarantees every slot you overwrite has already been read — this back-to-front trick is the reusable idea, and it reappears anywhere you do in-place array shifting.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you notice that front-to-back merging overwrites unread data in nums1, and pivot to filling from the back — the insight that makes O(1) space possible.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Merging front-to-back into nums1, clobbering values you haven't compared yet, or looping on nums1.length (which includes the padding zeros) instead of m.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the naive copy-and-sort, explain why a forward merge corrupts nums1, then derive the back-to-front pointers and note the loop can stop once nums2 is drained.

problemStatement:
You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, sorted in **non-decreasing order**, and two integers `m` and `n` representing the number of elements in `nums1` and `nums2` respectively.

**Merge** `nums1` and `nums2` into a single array sorted in non-decreasing order.

The final sorted array should **not** be returned by the function, but instead be *stored inside the array* `nums1`. To accommodate this, `nums1` has a length of `m + n`, where the first `m` elements are the ones that should be merged, and the last `n` elements are set to `0` and should be ignored. `nums2` has a length of `n`.
understanding: nums1 is over-allocated: its real data is the first m slots, and the last n slots are padding zeros that exist only to give us room. We must end with nums1 holding all m+n values in sorted order — in place, no return value.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are both arrays guaranteed sorted on entry?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, both are non-decreasing. That's what makes a linear merge possible — if they weren't, we'd have to sort.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the trailing space in nums1 always exactly n zeros?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. nums1.length == m + n by definition, and the last n entries are placeholders to ignore. Use m and n, not nums1.length.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can m or n be zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. If n == 0 there's nothing to merge; if m == 0, nums1 should just become a copy of nums2. The back-to-front loop handles both naturally.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the result be O(1) extra space?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's the expected answer. Copy-and-sort passes the judge but signals you missed the in-place merge the problem is built to test.

examples.explanation: Merging [1,2,3] and [2,5,6] gives [1,2,2,3,5,6], written back into nums1.
nums2 is empty, so nums1 is already the answer — the loop never runs.
nums1 has no real elements; the single value from nums2 fills the only slot.

approaches.name: Copy and Sort (Naive)
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to show you have a working baseline — then immediately note it ignores the sorted inputs and the free space.
hints: You already have all m+n values living in nums1 (the real ones up front, zeros at the back). What if you just put nums2's values into those zero slots?
Copy each nums2[j] into nums1[m + j], so all m+n values sit in nums1.
Now nums1 holds everything but out of order — call a standard sort and let it fix the arrangement.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Copying nums2 is O(n); the dominating cost is sorting m+n elements at O((m+n)log(m+n)). The sort is in-place (Java's dual-pivot quicksort on primitives, Python's Timsort), so no asymptotic extra space beyond the call stack.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal way to satisfy the spec: physically place all the data in one array, then sort it. Copy `nums2[j]` into `nums1[m + j]` for each `j`, so the trailing zero region now holds `nums2`'s values, and finish with a library sort over the whole length.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The problem says *"store the result inside nums1"*. The simplest reading is: get every value into `nums1` somehow, then make `nums1` sorted. We don't have to think about merge logic at all — we lean on the sorting routine to do the ordering for us. It's correct, it's short, and it's a fine sanity-check answer to state out loud.

**Why it leaves value on the table.** Both inputs arrive *already sorted*. A general-purpose sort throws that information away and re-discovers the order from scratch at `O((m+n)log(m+n))`. A merge exploits the existing order and runs in `O(m+n)` — strictly better. Whenever you sort data that's already partially ordered, an interviewer hears *"I didn't use the structure I was given."*

**Why the copy targets `m + j`.** The first `m` slots hold real data we must not clobber, and the next `n` slots are the zeros. Writing `nums2[j]` to `nums1[m + j]` drops each `nums2` value neatly into the padding region, so after the copy `nums1` contains exactly the `m+n` values we need — just unsorted across the seam.

**Why we don't ship this.** It works and even passes the judge, but the entire point of the problem is the in-place linear merge. Mention this as your baseline, state its `log` factor, and then reach for three pointers.
approaches.insight: The sorted-ness of the inputs is the gift the problem hands you. Any solution that calls a comparison sort is implicitly admitting it ignored that gift — a strong cue to look for a linear merge instead.

dryRun.intro: Drop nums2 into the trailing zeros, then sort the whole array.

Sorts all m+n values — this is the O((m+n)log(m+n)) step that ignores the existing order.

Timsort over all values — works, but discards the fact the inputs were already sorted.

edgeCases.behavior: The copy loop never runs; sort over the already-sorted m elements is a no-op cost.
All n values are copied to indices 0..n-1, then sorted — equivalent to copying nums2.

pitfalls: Looping the copy to n but writing to nums1[j] instead of nums1[m + j] — overwrites real data.
Sorting only part of the array (e.g. Arrays.sort(nums1, 0, m)) — leaves nums2's values unsorted.
Mentioning only this approach — interviewers want the O(m+n) merge.

approaches.name: Three Pointers, Back to Front (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'fill the tail with the larger element so we never overwrite unread data'.
hints: A forward merge into nums1 would overwrite nums1's own unread values. Where in nums1 is there guaranteed-empty space you can safely write into right now?
The free slots are at the END of nums1. So fill from the back: keep a write pointer k at index m+n-1 and compare the current largest of each array.

Use i = m-1, j = n-1, k = m+n-1. At each step write the larger of nums1[i] and nums2[j] into nums1[k], decrement that source pointer and k. Stop when j hits -1; remaining nums1 values are already in place.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the m+n slots is written exactly once and each comparison is O(1), so total work is O(m+n). We only use a handful of index variables → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk both arrays from their high ends and fill `nums1` from its high end. Keep `i = m−1` (last real value in `nums1`), `j = n−1` (last value in `nums2`), and `k = m+n−1` (the final slot). At each step copy the **larger** of `nums1[i]` and `nums2[j]` into `nums1[k]`, then step that source pointer and `k` back by one.

**Why back-to-front is the whole trick.** Picture a forward merge writing into `nums1[0]`, `nums1[1]`, … The very first write could land on `nums1[0]`, a value we still need to compare later — we'd destroy input before reading it, which is exactly why a naive in-place forward merge is impossible without a buffer. Now flip direction. The slots from index `m` to `m+n−1` are *padding* — nothing real lives there. If we always write the current largest remaining value into the highest empty slot, the write head `k` stays strictly ahead of (to the right of) both read heads `i` and `j`. Every slot we overwrite is one we've already consumed or one that was padding to begin with. That positional guarantee is what makes `O(1)` space possible.

**Why we compare and take the larger.** We're constructing the sorted array from its **largest** element down. The largest unplaced value must be one of the two current candidates at the read heads (everything to their left is smaller, since both arrays are sorted). So `nums1[k]` should receive `max(nums1[i], nums2[j])`, and we retreat the pointer we drew from. Filling largest-first is the mirror image of a normal forward merge that fills smallest-first.

**Why the loop ends when `j` reaches −1.** Two cases at termination. If `nums1` empties first (`i < 0`) while `nums2` still has values, we must keep copying `nums2`'s remaining values down — so the loop has to continue while `j >= 0`. But if `nums2` empties first (`j < 0`), every remaining `nums1` value is *already sitting in its correct position* at the front of `nums1` — they were never moved, so there's nothing left to do. That asymmetry is why the canonical loop condition is `while (j >= 0)` and why the `i >= 0` test lives *inside* the comparison: it stops us from reading `nums1[-1]` once `nums1` is exhausted.

**Why this beats copy-and-sort.** No auxiliary array, no `log` factor — each value is touched once. It's the textbook merge step of merge sort, specialised to reuse `nums1`'s tail as the output buffer.
approaches.insight: The free space lives at the back, so write at the back. The deeper, reusable idea: when you must overwrite an array in place, choose a fill direction where your write pointer can never collide with an unread read pointer. Here that direction is right-to-left; in other shifting problems it might be left-to-right — the principle is the same.

java.explanation: Write head starts at the LAST slot — the free space is at the tail, so we fill backwards.
Loop until nums2 is drained; leftover nums1 values are already in their correct positions.
Guard i >= 0 so we never read nums1[-1] after nums1 empties; take the LARGER candidate.
Place the larger value at the tail and retreat both the source and write pointers.

python.explanation: Write head at the last index — fill from the back into the padding region.
Stop when nums2 is exhausted; remaining nums1 prefix is already sorted in place.
The i >= 0 guard short-circuits before indexing, avoiding a wrap-around read at -1.
Copy the larger candidate into the current tail slot.

diagrams.title: Write head stays ahead of read heads
diagrams.caption: k is always at or right of both i and j, so each overwrite hits consumed or padding space.

frames.action: j exhausted → [1,2] untouched and already correct

edgeCases.behavior: i starts at -1, so the i>=0 guard fails and every write comes from nums2 → nums1 becomes [1].
j starts at -1, the while loop never executes, nums1 is left untouched (already correct).

pitfalls: Filling front-to-back into nums1 — overwrites unread values and needs a buffer.
Forgetting the i >= 0 guard — crashes or wraps when nums1 empties before nums2.
Using nums1.length instead of m+n-1 for k — they're equal here, but relying on the padding region's size in other ways is fragile.
Stopping the loop when i < 0 instead of when j < 0 — drops the remaining nums2 values.

commonMistakes: Merging into nums1 from the front, clobbering values not yet compared.
Iterating to nums1.length and merging the padding zeros as if they were data.
Dropping the i >= 0 guard, causing an out-of-bounds read when nums1 empties first.
Looping while i >= 0 instead of while j >= 0 — leftover nums2 values get lost.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forward merge overwrites unread data
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Writing the merged result into nums1 starting at index 0 stomps on nums1's own values before they're compared. The first write to nums1[0] can destroy a value you still need.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the i >= 0 guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When nums1 runs out first, i becomes -1. Reading nums1[i] then indexes nums1[-1] — a crash in Java, a wrap-around read in Python. The guard must be checked before the comparison.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating padding zeros as real values
commonMistakesDetailed.why: nums1.length is m+n, but only the first m entries are data. Looping over nums1.length and comparing the trailing zeros merges fake values into the result.

patternNote: Canonical in-place merge filled back-to-front. Recognise it whenever you must combine sorted data into a buffer that already holds one input — choose the fill direction that keeps the write head clear of unread reads. Same backward-fill idea powers Squares of a Sorted Array and the merge step of merge sort.
